analysis.one_liner: Replaces private corporate audits with an annual government audit of every public company.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House Financial Services subcommittee until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced during the wave of corporate accounting scandals, would have created a Federal Bureau of Audits inside the SEC to audit the financial statements of every publicly traded company each year. Its stated premise was that auditors hired by the companies they audit face a built-in conflict of interest. It would have banned bureau employees from working for audited companies for ten years, let the SEC set auditing standards, and charged public companies a fee to cover the bureau's roughly $5.15 billion first-year budget.
analysis.who_benefits: Small investors and employees whose savings depend on accurate corporate financial statements. The bill's findings say failed audits cost investors billions of dollars when restatements sent stock prices tumbling, and it argues that only a government agency, not a firm hired and fired by its client, can provide a truly independent audit.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Federal Bureau of Audits within the SEC to conduct an annual audit of the financial statements of every reporting issuer [S2][S3].

Removes the auditors' conflict of interest: bureau personnel would be independent of SEC supervision of other functions, and former bureau employees could not take jobs or pay from companies they audited, or from accountants serving them, for ten years [S2][S3].

Current bureau employees must hold investments in blind trusts, and the bill's findings state that accounting firms' conflicts of interest pressured auditors to sign off on substandard financial statements that cost investors billions [S3].
Finances the bureau entirely through fees on the companies it audits rather than through general taxpayer funding [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies, which would pay fees covering the bureau's operations — $5.15 billion appropriated for the first fiscal year — and lose their ability to hire and fire their own auditors. Accounting firms would lose the entire market for public-company audits.

drawbacks.text: The fee burden is large: the bill appropriates $5.15 billion for the bureau's first year, collected from reporting issuers, a cost that companies would pass on to shareholders [S3].

It replaces the entire private audit industry for public companies with a government monopoly, a dramatic expansion of federal power over financial reporting whose cost, staffing, and audit quality are untested; the bill itself exempts bureau auditors from civil service pay to match private-sector salaries [S3].

Good-faith objection: an independent, self-funded oversight board with rules for auditor independence could address the conflict of interest without a government takeover of all audits — the approach Congress ultimately took later in 2002 with a private-sector oversight board (general knowledge).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem it targeted was real and large — audit failures had cost investors billions, and auditors were hired and fired by the very companies they checked. The bill's remedy was the most aggressive one available: government employees auditing every public company, funded by a multibillion-dollar fee. That solves the conflict of interest outright but at high cost and with real risks about how well a new government bureau could perform thousands of complex annual audits. More modest independence rules could have captured much of the benefit at far less cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its Capital Markets subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on February 26, 2002, joined by Reps. Sanders and Filner, during the period when corporate accounting failures were costing investors billions of dollars [S3][S5].

The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee the same day, and on March 18, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].
The committee never acted on the bill even though its own findings documented the problem: auditors hired and fired by their clients, implicated in failed audits that cost investors billions [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Accounting firms kept their audit business and their ability to be hired by the companies they audited, and public companies avoided the new audit fees. Investors and employees gained nothing from this bill, though Congress later enacted a narrower audit oversight law that year.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican supported the bill [S4].

industries.note: The bill would replace private audits of public companies with government audits, eliminating the firms' entire public-company audit business. The bill's own findings say their client-hiring relationship pressured auditors to approve substandard financials that cost investors billions [S3].

Companies would pay a fee covering roughly $5.15 billion in first-year bureau costs and lose control over hiring their own auditors. Executives benefit from approval over their auditors; their shareholders and employees are the ones misled when audits fail [S3].
